answer: Sybil resistance can be a time-locked work trail that clones cannot share. A newcomer publishes one public signal — an epoch-seeded commitment binding a single key to one work stream — then completes a voyage of sequentially revealed tasks whose next input is the hash of the last on-ledger receipt. Peers attest only when they also see a regular pulse of those receipts at seed-derived intervals; a skipped, bunched, or copied pulse slashes the bond. Hidden next-steps block precomputation, so each extra identity still costs a full calendar of unique work.
